passages.title: A Seed's Journey
passages.text:
A Seed's Journey

Many plants begin life as seeds. A seed contains a tiny plant and stored food that can help it begin to grow. Most seeds also have a protective covering. Before a seed can sprout, it usually needs suitable warmth and water. Many seeds also need air. A seed will not grow well if it is kept too dry, flooded for too long or placed where conditions are unsuitable.

At Meadow View School, the gardening club wanted to grow native wildflowers beside a path. Their teacher, Mr Sen, helped them read the instructions on a packet and learn about the plants before they began. The packet explained that the seeds should be sown in loose soil in a sunny place. The children first removed litter and small weeds from the chosen patch. An adult checked that the area was safe and that the plants would not block the path.

The club loosened the soil with small hand tools and scattered the seeds carefully. They covered them with a thin layer of soil, following the packet's advice. Some seeds were tiny, so the children mixed them with a little dry sand to help spread them more evenly. They watered the patch gently. The soil became moist, but they avoided pouring on so much water that it formed puddles.

The children made a simple observation chart. Each week, they recorded rainfall, the condition of the soil and any changes they could see. At first, nothing appeared above the ground. A few children thought the seeds had failed, but Mr Sen explained that roots often begin growing before a shoot can be seen. After several days, small green shoots appeared in parts of the patch. Not every seed sprouted, and the children learned that seeds can differ in age and condition and that local conditions also matter.

As the plants grew, the club checked whether the soil was drying out and removed weeds carefully. They did not pull up every unfamiliar plant at once; they compared what they saw with their guide and asked an adult when they were uncertain. The children also noticed that some seedlings grew more strongly where sunlight reached the soil for longer.

By the end of the term, several wildflowers had grown tall enough to produce buds. The club left space around the plants and kept a record of which areas grew best. They understood that a garden does not appear in a day: choosing suitable seeds, preparing the ground, giving steady care and observing changes all help. Their chart also showed that careful records can answer questions better than a quick guess.
